concept.title: What is Cloud Storage?
concept.shortdesc: Describes types of cloud storage and services and their associated security threats.

conbody.p: Cloud storage enables individuals and organizations to store, access, and manage data via the Internet, removing the need for local drives or in-house servers. Fundamentally, it virtualizes physical infrastructure into a shared pool of offsite resources. When a file is uploaded, it travels securely — typically using encryption protocols like TLS — to a cloud endpoint, where it’s distributed across multiple backend systems and saved with built-in redundancy to protect against data loss.

A “cloud storage device” can refer to client-side applications that map a remote storage bucket as a virtual drive, or to software-defined storage nodes on the provider’s side. By abstracting hardware details, they let users treat cloud storage as if it were a local disk, simplifying integration with existing workflows.

Cloud storage services are categorized by how they organize and present data. The three main models — file, block, and object storage — each address different performance, scalability, and application requirements.

section.title: File Storage
section.p: File storage presents data as a hierarchical file-and-folder structure, accessible via standard protocols like Network File System (NFS) or Server Message Block (SMB).

section.title: Block Storage
section.p: Block storage exposes raw storage volumes — via iSCSI or Fibre Channel — to virtual machines or physical servers. Each volume appears as a local disk, allowing operating systems and databases to format it with their preferred file system.

section.title: Object Storage
section.p: Object storage stores data as discrete objects within a flat, globally unique namespace, accessed through RESTful APIs (for example, the Amazon S3 API). Each object combines data, metadata (key–value pairs that describe the object), and a unique identifier.
section.note: Securing data in the cloud involves guarding against breaches, unauthorized access, and external attacks. While cloud providers invest heavily in robust defenses, organizations must understand how security responsibilities are shared and implemented.
